Movies about computers AI or hacking.Top Gun: A 1986 film about Navy fighter pilots, famous for Kenny Loggins' Danger Zone, not about computers.

Final Fantasy characters.Cloud: The spiky-haired mercenary of Final Fantasy VII wields the huge Buster Sword, and his identity crisis is central to the story.
Final Fantasy characters.Tifa: Cloud's childhood friend in Final Fantasy VII is a martial artist, and her brawling style stands apart from the swordsmen around her.
Final Fantasy characters.Aerith: Her death in Final Fantasy VII in 1997 remains one of gaming's most famous shocks, and her name was originally Aeris in English.
Final Fantasy characters.Sephiroth: The silver-haired villain of Final Fantasy VII, whose theme One-Winged Angel features Latin choir chanting, also appears in Smash Bros.
Final Fantasy characters.Squall: The brooding hero of Final Fantasy VIII wields a gunblade, a sword with a revolver mechanism, and he leads the SeeD mercenaries.
Final Fantasy characters.Lightning: The pink-haired soldier is the heroine of Final Fantasy XIII, and her real name is Claire Farron.
Final Fantasy characters.Tidus: The blitzball star of Final Fantasy X narrates the game, and his laugh in an early scene became a meme.
Final Fantasy characters.Yuna: This summoner in Final Fantasy X goes on a pilgrimage to fight Sin, and she returned in a direct sequel, a rarity for the series.
Final Fantasy characters.Zidane: The tailed thief of Final Fantasy IX is a member of the Tantalus troupe, and he returns to the stage in the game's opening.
Final Fantasy characters.Vivi: This young black mage of Final Fantasy IX, who worries about his short life, is among the series' most beloved characters.
Final Fantasy characters.Barret: The gun-armed leader of AVALANCHE in Final Fantasy VII replaces his right hand with a gun.
Final Fantasy characters.Noctis: The prince of Final Fantasy XV travels by car with his three friends, and the game started life as Final Fantasy Versus XIII.
Final Fantasy characters.Kefka: The jester villain of Final Fantasy VI is famous for his laugh, and he actually succeeds in destroying the world.
Final Fantasy characters.Link: The green-clad hero of Hyrule is Nintendo's, and he is a silent protagonist, the opposite of Final Fantasy's talkative casts.
Final Fantasy characters.Zelda: The series is named for the princess, not the hero Link, a common mix-up, and she belongs to Nintendo's Hyrule.
Final Fantasy characters.Ganondorf: The Zelda series' main villain usually turns up as the Gerudo king, and he belongs to Nintendo.
Final Fantasy characters.Samus: Metroid's bounty hunter was revealed as a woman at the end of the 1986 game, but she is from Nintendo.
Final Fantasy characters.Solid Snake: The Metal Gear hero was created by Hideo Kojima at Konami, and he is not a Final Fantasy character.
Final Fantasy characters.Kratos: The Spartan of God of War is from Sony Santa Monica, and he is not from Final Fantasy.
Final Fantasy characters.Dante: The devil hunter of Devil May Cry is from Capcom, and his name is a nod to Dante Alighieri.
Final Fantasy characters.Leon Kennedy: He is the Resident Evil rookie cop from Capcom, and not a character from Final Fantasy.
Final Fantasy characters.Jill Valentine: The Resident Evil heroine was a Capcom character and escaped the Spencer Mansion in the 1996 original.
Final Fantasy characters.Geralt: CD Projekt's white-haired witcher, from Andrzej Sapkowski's novels, belongs to another series.
Final Fantasy characters.Ezio: The Renaissance assassin of Assassin's Creed II is a Ubisoft hero, and he is not in Final Fantasy.

Books by Dr. Seuss.The Cat in the Hat: Published in 1957, it was written using a limited list of about 236 simple words, after a publisher challenged Seuss to replace boring school readers.
Books by Dr. Seuss.Green Eggs and Ham: Seuss wrote it to win a bet with publisher Bennett Cerf, who doubted he could finish a book using only 50 different words. He won.
Books by Dr. Seuss.The Lorax: The Once-ler's greed fells every Truffula tree, and the book ends with a single carved word, UNLESS, urging readers to act.
Books by Dr. Seuss.Horton Hears a Who!: 'A person's a person, no matter how small,' says Horton about the tiny Whos, and Seuss dedicated the 1954 book to a Japanese friend.
Books by Dr. Seuss.Fox in Socks: This 1965 tongue-twister marathon has Mr. Knox begging the fox to stop as the rhymes get harder and harder.
Books by Dr. Seuss.Hop on Pop: Seuss's 1963 beginner book includes the rule 'STOP! You must not hop on pop,' a joke that some parents reportedly took seriously.
Books by Dr. Seuss.Yertle the Turtle: A 1958 fable of a king who stacks turtles into a throne, often read as a swipe at dictators. The lowest turtle topples him with a burp.
Books by Dr. Seuss.The Sneetches: Star-bellied Sneetches look down on plain-bellied ones until a salesman's machines make the difference meaningless. It is Seuss's 1953 lesson on prejudice.
Books by Dr. Seuss.If I Ran the Zoo: The 1950 book where the word 'nerd' is believed to have first appeared in print, as the name of a grumpy creature.
Books by Dr. Seuss.Goodnight Moon: Margaret Wise Brown's 1947 bedtime classic says goodnight to every object in a 'great green room'. Not by Seuss.
Books by Dr. Seuss.The Gruffalo: Julia Donaldson's mouse-and-monster tale is rhymed like Seuss, but it is a British book from 1999.
Books by Dr. Seuss.Curious George: H. A. and Margret Rey, Jewish refugees, escaped Paris by bicycle in 1940 carrying the monkey's manuscript.
Books by Dr. Seuss.Corduroy: Don Freeman's 1968 story of a department-store teddy bear hunting for his lost button has nothing to do with Seuss.
Books by Dr. Seuss.Madeline: Ludwig Bemelmans opened this 1939 tale with 'In an old house in Paris that was covered with vines'. Not Seuss.
Books by Dr. Seuss.The Snowy Day: Ezra Jack Keats's 1962 book was among the first mainstream picture books with a Black child as hero, and won the Caldecott Medal.
Books by Dr. Seuss.Strega Nona: Tomie dePaola's Italian tale of a pasta pot that won't stop cooking is a Caldecott Honor book, not a Seuss.
Books by Dr. Seuss.Pat the Bunny: Dorothy Kunhardt's 1940 touch-and-feel book, in which you pat a real fuzzy bunny, is often called the first of its kind.
Books by Dr. Seuss.The Polar Express: Chris Van Allsburg's 1985 tale of a magical train to the North Pole won the Caldecott Medal in 1986.
Books by Dr. Seuss.Stellaluna: Janell Cannon's 1993 story of a baby fruit bat raised by birds is a gentle nature tale, not by Seuss.
Books by Dr. Seuss.Olivia: Ian Falconer's 2000 pig is drawn mostly in black, white and red, a style far from Seuss's wild colors.
Books by Dr. Seuss.Frog and Toad: Arnold Lobel's gentle early-reader series about two amphibian friends includes a Newbery Honor winner, Frog and Toad Together.
Books by Dr. Seuss.Blueberries for Sal: Robert McCloskey's 1948 tale has a girl and a bear cub mixing up their mothers while picking berries in Maine.
Books by Dr. Seuss.Owl Moon: Jane Yolen's quiet story of a father and child going owling won the Caldecott Medal for John Schoenherr's art.
Books by Dr. Seuss.Swimmy: Leo Lionni's 1963 tale has a small black fish teach his school to swim together in the shape of one huge fish.

Things invisible to the human eye.Air: Air is about 78 percent nitrogen and 21 percent oxygen, and a liter of it weighs over a gram.
Things invisible to the human eye.Wind: We never see wind itself, only the leaves, dust and waves it pushes around.
Things invisible to the human eye.Sound waves: Sound travels at about 343 meters per second in air, and faster in water and steel.
Things invisible to the human eye.Radio waves: Radio waves are the same kind of electromagnetic wave as light, only with much longer wavelengths.
Things invisible to the human eye.Oxygen: Pure oxygen gas is colorless, though liquid oxygen is a pale blue.
Things invisible to the human eye.Gravity: Gravity can't be seen, only its effects; Einstein described it as the curving of spacetime.
Things invisible to the human eye.Ultraviolet light: Bees see ultraviolet light, and many flowers have UV patterns that act as landing guides invisible to us.
Things invisible to the human eye.Wi-Fi signal: Wi-Fi uses radio waves at 2.4 and 5 GHz, and the 2.4 GHz band is shared with microwave ovens.
Things invisible to the human eye.Infrared: Pit vipers sense infrared as heat, and thermal cameras use it to see in total darkness.
Things invisible to the human eye.X-rays: X-rays were discovered in 1895 by Wilhelm Röntgen, who soon made an image of his wife's hand.
Things invisible to the human eye.Carbon monoxide: Carbon monoxide is colorless and odorless, which is why it is called the silent killer and detectors are vital.
Things invisible to the human eye.Smoke: Smoke is made of tiny solid and liquid particles that scatter light, so you can see it clearly.
Things invisible to the human eye.Fog: Fog is a cloud at ground level, made of visible water droplets.
Things invisible to the human eye.Rainbow: A rainbow is visible light split by raindrops, so you can see it even though you can never touch it.
Things invisible to the human eye.Shadow: A shadow is where light is blocked, and you see it as a dark patch.
Things invisible to the human eye.Lightning: Lightning is a glowing channel of superheated plasma, and the flash lasts only a fraction of a second.
Things invisible to the human eye.Cloud: Clouds are visible collections of tiny water droplets or ice crystals.
Things invisible to the human eye.Dust: Dust becomes striking in a sunbeam because each speck scatters light toward your eye.
Things invisible to the human eye.Mist: Mist is a thin version of fog, with droplets that are visible, and visibility stays above one kilometer.
Things invisible to the human eye.Window glass: Glass is transparent, not invisible; it reflects some light, which is why birds still hit windows.
Things invisible to the human eye.Soap bubble: A soap bubble's swirling colors come from light interfering within its ultra-thin film.
Things invisible to the human eye.Spider web: Spider silk is thin but visible, especially when dew clings to it, and it is stronger than steel by weight.
Things invisible to the human eye.Flame: A flame is glowing hot gas and soot, so we see it even though it isn't a solid thing.
Things invisible to the human eye.Hologram: A hologram is a 3D image recorded with laser light, and you can see it plainly.

Things you'd see at a harbor.Lighthouse: The Pharos of Alexandria, built in the 3rd century BC, was among the Seven Wonders and may have stood over 100 meters tall.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Pier: Piers jut out from shore to let boats dock, and Santa Monica's 1909 pier is one of the best-known in California.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Jetty: A jetty extends out to protect a harbor entrance from waves and currents, and the word comes from the French for thrown.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Crane: Harbor cranes can lift containers weighing tens of tonnes, and modern ones can serve ships carrying over 20,000 boxes.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Tugboat: Tugboats are small but powerful, and a strong tug can push or tow a ship hundreds of times its own weight.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Buoy: Buoys mark channels and hazards, and by international convention red and green ones show which side to pass on, depending on region.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Bollard: Ships tie up to bollards, which are strong posts, and some on old quays are made from recycled cannons.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Dock: Dock can mean a berth or an enclosed basin, and dry docks let workers drain water to repair a ship's hull.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Fishing boat: Many harbors still land fish at dawn, and some towns auction the day's catch right on the quay.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Seagull: Seagulls scavenge harbors for scraps, and they can drink salt water thanks to glands that excrete the excess salt.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Breakwater: A breakwater is an offshore barrier that calms the water inside the harbor, and some are made of huge concrete blocks.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Runway: Runways belong at airports, and the longest in the world, at Qamdo Bamda in Tibet, is about 5.5 kilometers.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Taxiway: Taxiways link runways to terminals, and they sit at airports rather than harbors.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Pit lane: Pit lanes are where race cars stop for fuel and tires, and F1 crews can change all four wheels in under three seconds.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Ski lift: Ski lifts belong at snowy resorts, and some mountain gondolas can carry thousands of people an hour.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Haystack: Haystacks are found on farms, and farmers piled hay into them to store winter feed for livestock.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Cattle grid: A cattle grid is a road gap with bars that animals won't cross, which saves farmers from needing a gate.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Paddock: A paddock is a small enclosed field for horses, and at racetracks it is where horses are shown before races.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Cactus: Cacti mostly grow in the Americas' deserts, and they store water in thick stems so they can survive droughts.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Treehouse: A treehouse perches among branches, and some, like those in Papua New Guinea's Korowai region, stand high above the ground.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Barn: A barn stores crops and shelters animals, and the iconic red color came from cheap iron oxide paint farmers mixed with oil.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Cornfield: A cornfield is farmland, and a single corn plant can grow over two meters in a season, but not near docks.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Stalactite: A stalactite hangs from a cave ceiling and grows only a few millimeters per decade, so harbors won't have one.
Things you'd see at a harbor.Igloo: Igloos are Arctic snow shelters that stand on ice, not harbors, and they depend on cold, packed snow.

Famous highways and long-distance routes.Route 66: Nicknamed the Mother Road, it ran from Chicago to Santa Monica and was officially decommissioned in 1985, replaced by interstates.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Silk Road: Less one road than a web of trade routes linking China to the Mediterranean; the name was coined by a German geographer in the 1800s.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Appian Way: Begun in 312 BC, this Roman road ran from Rome toward southern Italy, and parts of its original paving stones still survive.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Trans-Canada Highway: At roughly 7,800 km from coast to coast, it is among the longest national highways in the world and was finished in 1962.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Autobahn: Germany's motorway network famously has stretches with no general speed limit, though a recommended speed of 130 km/h applies.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Great Ocean Road: Built by returned soldiers after World War I, this Victorian coastal route is a memorial and passes the Twelve Apostles rock stacks.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Karakoram Highway: Linking Pakistan and China across the Khunjerab Pass at about 4,700 m, it is one of the highest paved international roads on Earth.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Grand Trunk Road: One of South Asia's oldest and longest roads, it stretches from Bangladesh to Afghanistan and was upgraded by Sher Shah Suri in the 1500s.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Lincoln Highway: Opened in 1913, it was among the first transcontinental roads for cars in the US, running from New York to San Francisco.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Stelvio Pass: This Italian Alpine pass climbs through 48 hairpin bends on its northern side, and is a bucket-list drive for cyclists and car fans.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Trans-Siberian: A trap: this is a railway, not a road. At about 9,300 km from Moscow to Vladivostok, it is the longest railway line in the world.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Panama Canal: A trap: it is a waterway, not a road. Ships are lifted about 26 m above sea level by locks to cross the isthmus.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Suez Canal: A shipping canal, not a highway. Opened in 1869, it lets ships skip the long trip around Africa between Europe and Asia.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Hadrian's Wall: A Roman defensive wall across northern England begun around AD 122; it is a barrier, not a long-distance road, though walkers now follow its path.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Mississippi: A river, not a road. Its name comes from an Ojibwe phrase meaning great river, and it drains about a third of the continental US.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Danube: A river, not a road: it flows through ten countries, more than any other river in the world.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Channel Tunnel: A rail tunnel, not a highway; its undersea section under the English Channel is about 38 km long, among the longest in the world.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Eurostar: A high-speed passenger train service, not a road. It has linked London with Paris and Brussels through the Channel Tunnel since 1994.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Amazon: A river, not a road. It carries more water than any other river, and for long stretches no bridge crosses it.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Thames: A river, not a road. Despite being modest in length, it is tidal as far upstream as Teddington, west of central London.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Appalachian Trail: A footpath, not a road: about 3,500 km of marked trail through 14 states, and cars are not allowed on it.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Orient Express: A famous luxury train, not a highway. It launched in 1883 and later inspired Agatha Christie's murder mystery.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Grand Canal: China's Grand Canal is a man-made waterway of about 1,800 km, so a canal rather than a road, and it is the world's longest.
Famous highways and long-distance routes.Hudson: A river, not a road. Henry Hudson explored it in 1609, and it runs from the Adirondacks down to New York Harbor.

Fabric patterns.Plaid: In North America plaid means any crisscross pattern, while in Scotland it originally meant a blanket-like length of tartan cloth.
Fabric patterns.Paisley: Paisley comes from a Persian and Indian teardrop motif, and its name from the Scottish town where it was mass-produced in the 1800s.
Fabric patterns.Polka dot: The 'polka' in polka dot comes from the dance craze of the 1800s. The dots had nothing to do with the dance but the name sold the fabric.
Fabric patterns.Houndstooth: Houndstooth is a woven check of broken, pointed shapes, originally from Scottish wool. Its name refers to a dog's jagged teeth.
Fabric patterns.Pinstripe: Pinstripes are thin lines on suit fabric. They began as a banker's look in 1800s London and later appeared on baseball uniforms.
Fabric patterns.Argyle: Argyle is a diamond pattern named for the Campbell clan's tartan of Argyll, Scotland, and it popped up on socks and sweaters.
Fabric patterns.Chevron: A chevron is a row of V-shapes. The same shape appears as a military stripe badge, and on the road markings.
Fabric patterns.Herringbone: Herringbone is a zigzag pattern that looks like fish bones. The Romans used it for road paving.
Fabric patterns.Gingham: Gingham is a lightweight checked cloth, woven from pre-dyed threads. Its name may come from a Malay word for 'striped'.
Fabric patterns.Tartan: A tartan's crossing stripes are linked to Scottish clans, but the registry of designs now includes thousands of new patterns.
Fabric patterns.Floral: Floral prints are among the oldest fabric designs, and even the 1960s hippie era filled clothing with big flower prints.
Fabric patterns.Camouflage: Military camouflage patterns were inspired by artists. French painters in World War I were the first to be called 'camoufleurs'.
Fabric patterns.Leopard print: Leopard print became high fashion in the 1940s after Christian Dior showed it. Before that it signaled royalty or power.
Fabric patterns.Velvet: Velvet is a luxurious fabric with a soft pile, not a pattern. Once it was a royal fabric because weaving it was so slow.
Fabric patterns.Satin: Satin is a weave with a glossy surface, not a pattern. The name may come from the Chinese port Quanzhou, known in medieval Europe as Zaytun.
Fabric patterns.Denim: Denim is a sturdy twill cotton, the fabric of jeans. Its name comes from the French 'serge de Nîmes', meaning cloth from Nîmes.
Fabric patterns.Suede: Suede is leather with a soft napped surface. Its name comes from the French 'gants de Suède', Swedish gloves.
Fabric patterns.Chiffon: Chiffon is a sheer, light fabric, not a pattern. Its name comes from the French word for a rag.
Fabric patterns.Fleece: Fleece is a soft synthetic fabric, first made from recycled plastic bottles, so it is a material rather than a design.
Fabric patterns.Taffeta: Taffeta is a crisp, rustling fabric used for ball gowns. It is a material, not a design printed on cloth.
Fabric patterns.Jersey: Jersey is a stretchy knit fabric named after the Channel Island, where fishermen's sweaters were made.
Fabric patterns.Organza: Organza is a sheer, stiff fabric used for veils and gowns, a material rather than a design.
Fabric patterns.Muslin: Muslin is a loosely woven cotton, named after the city of Mosul. Tailors use it to test designs before cutting costly cloth.
Fabric patterns.Canvas: Canvas is a heavy plain-woven fabric. Its name comes from the Latin 'cannabis', since it was once woven from hemp.

American fashion brands.Ralph Lauren: Ralph Lauren, born Ralph Lifshitz in the Bronx, started in 1967 by selling wide neckties under the Polo name.
American fashion brands.Calvin Klein: Calvin Klein turned underwear and denim into sexy mass-market brands in the late 1970s and 1980s, with famous ads featuring Brooke Shields.
American fashion brands.Tommy Hilfiger: Tommy Hilfiger launched in 1985 with a red, white and blue logo and became big in the 1990s through hip-hop artists.
American fashion brands.Levi's: Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis patented riveted denim trousers in 1873, so the brand is among the oldest still making jeans.
American fashion brands.Gap: Founded in San Francisco in 1969, Gap began by selling jeans and records.
American fashion brands.Michael Kors: Michael Kors made his name for polished American sportswear, and was a judge on Project Runway.
American fashion brands.Coach: Founded in 1941 in a Manhattan loft, Coach began with leather goods, and baseball-glove leather inspired its earliest handbags.
American fashion brands.Tory Burch: Tory Burch started her label in 2004, and her ballet-flat with a double-T logo was a hit.
American fashion brands.Kate Spade: Kate Spade started in 1993 with simple, colourful handbags, and the designer became a household name.
American fashion brands.Vera Wang: Vera Wang was a figure skater and Vogue editor before she designed wedding dresses.
American fashion brands.Donna Karan: Donna Karan launched her label in 1984 and her 'Seven Easy Pieces' were built to work together.
American fashion brands.Old Navy: Opened in 1994, Old Navy is Gap's budget-friendly sister brand, aimed at families who want cheap, bright basics.
American fashion brands.Abercrombie & Fitch: Abercrombie & Fitch was founded in 1892 as an outfitter for hunters and explorers, and Theodore Roosevelt was once a customer.
American fashion brands.Burberry: Burberry is British, from London, and its trench coat dates back to World War I.
American fashion brands.Zara: Zara is Spanish, from Galicia, and its parent company Inditex is one of the world's biggest fashion retailers.
American fashion brands.H&M: H&M is Swedish and started as a women's clothing shop in Västerås in 1947.
American fashion brands.Uniqlo: Uniqlo is Japanese, and its name is short for Unique Clothing Warehouse.
American fashion brands.Gucci: Gucci is Italian, from Florence, and was founded in 1921.
American fashion brands.Chanel: Chanel is French, founded by Coco Chanel in Paris.
American fashion brands.Lacoste: Lacoste is French and uses a crocodile in memory of founder René Lacoste.
American fashion brands.Adidas: Adidas is German, from Herzogenaurach, and was founded by Adi Dassler.
American fashion brands.Puma: Puma is also German from Herzogenaurach and founded by Adi's brother Rudolf after a family split.
American fashion brands.Hugo Boss: Hugo Boss is German and based in Metzingen.
American fashion brands.Benetton: Benetton is Italian, from Treviso, and known for bright knitwear and provocative ad campaigns.

Real foods (not fictional).Toad in the hole: Real British comfort food: sausages baked in Yorkshire pudding batter. There's no toad, just the sausages poking out.
Real foods (not fictional).Bubble and squeak: Real: a British fry-up of leftover cabbage and potatoes, named for the sounds it supposedly makes while cooking.
Real foods (not fictional).Haggis: Scotland's national dish is made from sheep's offal, oatmeal and spices. It's piped in with bagpipes on Burns Night.
Real foods (not fictional).Kedgeree: Real: smoked fish, rice and eggs, a Victorian breakfast adapted from the Indian dish khichri.
Real foods (not fictional).Poutine: Quebec's fries with gravy and cheese curds. Fresh curds are meant to squeak against your teeth.
Real foods (not fictional).Pavlova: A real meringue dessert named for the ballerina Anna Pavlova. Australia and New Zealand still argue over who invented it.
Real foods (not fictional).Lamington: Real: an Australian sponge cake dipped in chocolate and coconut, named after a Queensland governor, Lord Lamington.
Real foods (not fictional).Natto: Real, a Japanese breakfast of sticky, stringy fermented soybeans. Its smell puts off many, but it's rich in vitamin K2.
